hook.text: In the 1970s, American cars broke down so often that owners joked 'Fix Or Repair Daily' about Ford.

buildup.text: Japanese cars weren't exciting, but they started every morning and rarely needed repairs.

discovery.text: The quality gap was measurable. Japanese cars had far fewer defects per vehicle off the assembly line.

twist.text: Detroit blamed cheap labor. The real reason was better processes—Toyota's methods, not Japan's wages.

climax.text: By the 1990s, reliability ratings became a major buying factor. Japan dominated every survey.

punchline.text: Reliability isn't glamorous, but it wins markets.

quiz.question: What was the real reason for Japanese car quality?

details.summary: Japanese automakers led a reliability revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, using quality management systems that dramatically reduced defects and raised customer expectations for all car brands.
details.whyItMatters: Before the reliability revolution, frequent breakdowns were accepted as normal. Japanese standards forced the entire industry to improve, benefiting consumers worldwide.
takeaways: Toyota and Honda consistently topped reliability surveys
Total Quality Management reduced defects per vehicle dramatically
American and European brands were forced to match Japanese standards

faq.question: Why were Japanese cars more reliable than American ones?
faq.answer: Japanese manufacturers adopted rigorous quality control systems like TQM and kaizen. Workers were empowered to stop production lines to fix problems, preventing defects from reaching customers.

faq.question: Have American and European cars caught up in reliability?
faq.answer: Largely yes. By the 2010s, most major brands achieved competitive reliability scores. However, Japanese brands still frequently lead reliability surveys due to their deeply embedded quality culture.
